protected_assets: Ephemeral ML-KEM-768 shared secrets and session keys
adversary_capabilities: Submitting malformed JSON, newline-injected IDs, or unauthorized read/protected_read requests
Replaying captured messages or substituting recipient fields
Modifying persisted state or backup bundles on disk
Attempting to use retired key versions or expired session tickets
threat_scenarios: Concurrent process race overwriting revocation or audit state
Audit log tampering or backup rollback to reactivate revoked identities
Message replay, recipient substitution, loss/reordering, and stale session resumption
Unapproved privilege escalation and lateral movement in service logs
security_controls: Deny-by-default authorization before resource access or ML-KEM-768 encapsulation
Cross-process fcntl.flock serialization + atomic fsync/os.replace persistence
SHA-256 hash-chained audit log verified on every read, revoke, audit, and protected_read
HMAC-SHA-256 + SHA-256 backup verification with anti-rollback revocation checks
ML-KEM-768 encapsulation + HMAC-SHA-256 proof with immediate secret erasure
HMAC-SHA-256 message authentication, recipient binding, seen_msg_ids replay cache, and OrderedChannel
Deterministic rule-based event detector with approval-context and clock-offset correction
residual_risks: State at rest in keyctl-state.json is unencrypted JSON; an attacker with full write access to state can rewrite the unkeyed SHA-256 audit chain from genesis
pqcrypto==0.4.0 on Python 3.12 is not yet verified locally (local runtime is Python 3.14.7 without pqcrypto)
NodeCluster is an in-process simulation, not a real distributed consensus system
Detector accuracy (1.0 F1) is measured only on the 22-event synthetic practice dataset
assumptions_and_constraints: Offline Linux judging container with Python 3.12, pqcrypto==0.4.0, and read-only root filesystem
Writable state directory provided via TRACK4_STATE_DIR or OS temp directory
